title: Best AI study apps for MBBS students
summary: Compare AI study apps for MBBS revision, with practical ways to rehearse a viva, check a diagram and turn flashcards into a written answer.
body_markdown:
For MBBS revision, choose Educato when you need repeated practice from your own lecture notes. Choose NotebookLM when you need to reconcile a lecture, a practical handout and the reading your department assigned. Before picking either, decide what the examiner could ask you to produce: naming a structure, drawing it and defending your identification aloud are different tasks.


Educato publishes this page and makes one of the apps on it. We list it where it fits, with its limits.


## How can I use AI to study for MBBS exams?


Start with the answer format your department uses and work backwards to the material you need. For a viva, prepare to answer a follow-up aloud. For a written paper, practise organising the answer on a blank sheet. For a spotter, keep the image and the reason for identification together.


1. **Educato, best for repeat practice between classes.** You can study from your own PDFs, slides, documents and note photos, with spaced-repetition flashcards, a daily plan and an AI tutor for explanations. This fits a student who can follow a demonstration but needs another chance to recall it later. **Limits.** Full access is paid. AI-generated material can contain errors, and a correct flashcard answer does not establish that you can recognise a specimen.
2. **NotebookLM, best for revising from a defined set of department readings.** You can ask questions about notebook sources and turn them into flashcards or an audio overview. That is useful when your practical manual gives a short instruction and your lecture notes explain its purpose. The limitation for a practical is that hearing an explanation leaves the actual observation and demonstration for you to practise.

### Turn a labelled diagram into an oral question


Suppose your anatomy notes include a labelled transverse section. Cover the title and labels. Ask a friend to point to a structure, then answer aloud using a name, an orientation and a visible relation. Have the friend ask, “What in this picture supports your answer?” If your only reason is that the label usually sits in the upper corner of the slide, you have found something worth practising.


Make a study prompt from the missing relation. Keep the original figure nearby and check that the feature you named is actually visible in this view. A description copied from another view can be perfectly plausible and useless for identifying this section. When you can answer, use a different department-approved figure of the same region. Give yourself credit for a reason that travels between figures, even if the second image takes longer.


### Use a notebook to resolve a disagreement in your notes


A lecture outline might put a step under “principle” while your practical record puts it under “procedure”. Before asking for a combined summary, write down what each heading is trying to answer. One may describe why an observation occurs, the other what you were asked to do. Ask separate questions of the material, then look up the passages yourself. Preserve the distinction in the answer you practise.


If the passages really do conflict, copy the precise wording and page reference into a question for your demonstrator. Keep that item out of your revision deck until it is settled. Seeing the same explanation several times makes it familiar, which can make an uncorrected card particularly hard to spot later. Use teaching diagrams and fictional cases for this exercise. Leave patient names, record numbers and ward photographs out of your personal study uploads.


## What is the best AI app for MBBS students preparing for a viva?


Choose Educato to rehearse answering from memory, or NotebookLM to compare the explanations in your viva notes. If you cannot recall the opening term without a cue, repeat short prompts from your notes. If you can name it but lose the thread at “why?”, look up the supporting passage and build a follow-up question around it.


Try this rehearsal with a classmate. Give them a practical topic and the explanation in your manual, then put your own copy away. Ask them to interrupt after your first claim and request the observation that supports it. They should record your wording as closely as possible. Afterwards, underline every word in your answer that points to something you could see or demonstrate. Revise the sentence where you made a conclusion without giving the evidence.


For a practical without a diagram, imagine the examiner asks why you locate a feature under low power before increasing the magnification. “Then I change objectives” gives the next step but leaves the question unanswered. Explain that the wider field makes it easier to find the feature and centre it. Now predict what happens if the feature starts near the edge. It can fall outside the narrower field even though the slide stays still.


Check that prediction on paper. Draw two circles around the same centre and put a dot inside the larger circle, just outside the smaller one. Cover the drawing and explain why the dot disappears. If you can do that aloud, you have an answer that still works when the examiner changes the starting position.


### How should I revise a long answer after using flashcards?


Write the question at the top of a blank page and sketch the headings before opening any cards. Put the diagram where it helps the explanation and label it from memory. Now inspect the headings. Could a reader follow the sequence without hearing the lecture? If your answer is a collection of correct terms with no connection between them, practise the transition between the terms. Another round of isolated definitions will give you little information about that weakness.


Compare the result with the teaching material, mark the exact omissions and decide what needs another attempt. A missing label can become a short recall prompt. A missing relationship deserves a question beginning with “how” or “why”. If the weakness is fitting the whole answer on paper, repeat the written task with the time your teacher allows. Let the attempted answer choose the revision method.


For help checking answer choices, read[how to make MCQs from lecture notes](https://www.educato.com/blog/posts/best-ai-apps-to-make-mcqs-from-your-notes) . For choosing a tool across subjects, see[the guide for Indian students](https://www.educato.com/blog/posts/best-ai-study-apps-for-indian-students) . You can[start a free account](https://www.educato.com/app/start) with a topic you already know well enough to check.
